Amortization is fine and 180 kernels is a lot, but neither matters if the overhead being removed is tiny. Measure the fraction first.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: You switch from a BERT-based reranker to an XLM-RoBERTa-based one and keep the same max_length. Which detail changes in packing?
options: The query is now placed after the document
There are no special tokens at all
The model accepts 1,024 positions automatically
The pair uses four special tokens and no segment ids, so one fewer document token fits
explain: XLM-RoBERTa packs a pair as <s> A </s></s> B </s> and does not use token type ids. Order and the max_length you pass stay the same; the budget for the document shrinks by one token.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: A colleague proposes caching cross-encoder scores for every (query, document) pair to remove reranking latency. When does this actually help?
options: Only for repeated exact queries (head queries) over an unchanged candidate set; the long tail of new queries still pays full cost
Always, because cross-encoder scores never change
Never, because the scores depend on batch size
Only if the model uses sigmoid outputs
explain: A score is a function of the exact query and document text. Caching works for frequent repeated queries, which Hofstatter et al. also note as the exception, but most queries in real traffic are unique and must be scored live.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.getrandbits(128)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
uuid.uuid1()
hash(time.time())
explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Do not hash passwords
Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
Use constant-time comparison
Retire SHA-1
explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: Your equivalence test asserts allclose on the logits with atol = 1e-3 and it passes. What has it established about the generated tokens?
options: They must be identical, since the logits agree to within 1e-3.
Very little on its own: a 1e-3 tolerance only protects an argmax whose top-2 margin exceeds 2e-3, and near-ties are far smaller than that.
They are identical as long as the temperature is 0.
Nothing, because allclose is never a valid comparison for logits.
explain: A tolerance d on logits preserves the top-2 ordering only when the gap exceeds 2d. With atol = 1e-3 the test is blind to every position whose margin is under 2e-3, and near-ties can be around 1e-06. A tolerance is usable when it is paired with the margin distribution; the problem is the missing margin check, not allclose itself.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: A teammate sets the network drop rate to 50% in every simulation run to "find more bugs". What is the likely effect?
options: More bugs found, since more faults always means more coverage
The cluster rarely makes progress, so the run explores a small, repetitive set of states
Determinism breaks, because drops are random
Nothing, because consensus tolerates any drop rate
explain: The FoundationDB paper explicitly tunes fault distributions to avoid an excessive fault rate that drives the system into a small state space. At 50% loss on every run the cluster mostly retries and times out; deep states such as long recoveries under load are rarely reached. Vary the rate per run instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: In the fixed workflow, why does the deploy job also need the production environment, when it already has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`?
options: The `if:` is cosmetic and GitHub ignores it
Environments make jobs run faster
The `if:` lives in the workflow file, which a branch can edit; the environment's branch rule and reviewers are enforced by GitHub outside the file, and the cloud role can require that environment
Environments are needed to use actions/checkout
explain: A condition written in the workflow is only as trustworthy as the file. A branch can delete it. Environment protection rules are settings the branch cannot change, and an OIDC trust on environment:production means the cloud refuses tokens from any other job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A job runs on a pull_request event and references the environment `staging`. What subject does GitHub put in its token?
options: repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request
repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/pull/1/merge
repo:ORG/REPO:environment:staging
repo:ORG/REPO
explain: GitHub's reference: the subject includes the environment name when the job references an environment, and includes pull_request only if the job does not reference one.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: A developer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_24` with no comment to silence the open-SSH finding. What should the pipeline enforce?
options: Nothing: skips are always fine
Delete all skip comments automatically
Disable CKV_AWS_24 everywhere
Skips must name a reason (and ideally an owner and an end date) and go through review like any exception
explain: Checkov's format includes a suppression comment after the check id. A skip without a reason is an unreviewed exception to policy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: A self-hosted runner is suspected of running attacker code. What is the right first containment step?
options: Delete suspicious files on it and keep using it
Take it offline and replace it from a clean image, then rotate every secret jobs on it could reach
Restart the runner service
Rename the runner
explain: A persistent runner can hide leftover processes and modified tools (the PyTorch case). Rebuilding from a known-good image is the only state you can trust; secrets that passed through it must be treated as stolen.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism
question: A disaggregated deployment meets TTFT easily but misses TPOT at high load, and decode GPUs are near their KV memory limit. What is the most sensible next change?
options: Increase the prefill batch size
Merge the pools back into a colocated deployment
Add prefill instances
Add decode capacity (more decode instances or more parallelism per decode instance)
explain: TPOT is decided by the decode side. Decode batch size is bounded by KV memory, and DistServe notes that scaling the decoding instance with model parallelism (or memory techniques like PagedAttention and GQA) lets it batch more. Extra prefill instances would just send more KV caches to an already full decode pool.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
question: An MBR shows exactly one partition, type 0xEE, covering the whole disk. What should your tool do next?
options: Report a single unformatted partition
Read the GPT header at LBA 1 and its partition entries; the MBR is only a protective placeholder
Treat the disk as wiped, since 0xEE marks erased space
Search for 0x55 0xAA signatures to find hidden MBRs
explain: Type 0xEE is the GPT protective MBR. The real partition table is the GPT starting at LBA 1 (signature EFI PART). It does not mean unformatted or wiped.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The USN change journal: a diary of every file change
question: The oldest record in a server's change journal is from three days ago. Your intrusion window starts two weeks ago. What do you write?
options: No files were changed before three days ago
The intruder deleted the journal
The journal does not cover the window; absence of earlier records says nothing about earlier activity
The server was rebuilt three days ago
explain: The journal is trimmed from the start once it exceeds its maximum size, so on a busy volume coverage is short. Deletion or a rebuild would need other evidence (for example a USN reset or a process event).

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
question: A registry key's last write time is 2026-03-02 14:28. Which statement is safe?
options: Every value under this key was written at 14:28
A user opened this key in regedit at 14:28
The key or at least one of its values was last modified at 14:28
The key was created at 14:28
explain: Microsoft defines it as the last time the key or any of its values was modified. It is per key, not per value, and it records modification, not viewing or creation.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
question: A live acquisition inevitably changes the running system. Which ACPO principle governs this?
options: Principle 1: no action should change data that may be relied on in court, so live acquisition is forbidden
Principle 3: only a second examiner may access live systems
Principle 4: the investigation lead must perform the acquisition
Principle 2: the person accessing original data must be competent and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions
explain: Principle 2 covers the case where accessing original data is necessary. Principle 1 is the default, not a ban; Principle 3 requires an audit trail; Principle 4 puts overall responsibility on the person in charge.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Why does KTO estimate $z_0$ from mismatched (prompt, other example's output) pairs instead of each example's own output?
options: Because own outputs are usually chosen to be clearly good or bad, so their rewards are unrepresentatively large
Because mismatched pairs need no forward pass
Because the own output's log-ratio is always zero
Because it makes the estimate unbiased
explain: The paper says matched outputs have often been deliberately picked as canonically good or bad, giving high-magnitude rewards that would skew the reference point. The mismatched estimate still costs an extra forward pass and is explicitly biased (clamping adds upward bias), but it is cheap and stable.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: A backfill uses insert-if-absent. A user deletes subscription S: the dual write deletes it from both stores. A backfill worker had read S from the old store just before the delete, and writes it to the new store just after. What happens?
options: S comes back to life in the new store, because after the delete there is no row to block the insert
Nothing: insert-if-absent skips S because it already exists
The insert fails with a foreign-key error
The old store also gets S back
explain: Insert-if-absent treats a missing row as never copied, but here it is missing because it was deleted. The fix is to remember deletes (a tombstone row or a version that marks deletion), or to order the copy against the change log so the delete is applied after the copied row.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: You are writing a script that teammates will run for years across kernel upgrades. It counts file opens per process. Which probe should you choose first?
options: kprobe:do_sys_openat2, because kprobes can reach any function
uprobe on libc's open wrapper
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat, because tracepoints are stable interfaces in the kernel source
profile:hz:99, because sampling has the lowest overhead
explain: Tracepoints are placed by kernel developers and meant to keep a stable interface. Internal function names that kprobes target can be renamed or change arguments between versions. A libc uprobe misses programs that make the syscall directly, and sampling would miss most opens.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A bpftrace script printing one line per network packet starts reporting lost events under load. What is the best fix?
options: Replace printf with a map aggregation such as @[comm] = count() or hist(), so per-event data stays in the kernel
Increase max_strlen
Switch the probe from tracepoint to kprobe
Run two copies of the script
explain: Lost events mean user space cannot drain the ring buffer fast enough. Raising perf_rb_pages only buys headroom; aggregating in a map removes the per-event traffic entirely.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: A post-training int8 model loses 30 points of accuracy. Inspecting one conv layer, you find output channel ranges from 0.003 to 4.0, and the converter used one scale per tensor. What is the cheapest fix to try first?
options: Switch to quantization-aware training
Increase the calibration set from 200 to 20,000 images
Quantize activations per channel
Use per-channel weight scales
explain: A 1,300x range spread across channels is the classic per-tensor failure. Per-channel weight scales fix it with no training, and the whitepaper shows they recover MobileNetV2 to within about 2 points. More calibration data affects activation ranges, not weight ranges. QAT works too but costs a training run.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
question: Which feature from the NCSC forensic guidance most directly lets you notice that an appliance's configuration was changed while its own logs were wiped?
options: A larger local disk
Disabling time synchronisation
A web console in more languages
A heartbeat sent off the box that carries a SHA256 digest of the current configuration
explain: The digest leaves the device regularly, so a change shows up in the SIEM even if the device's local log is later cleared. A larger disk still lives on the box the intruder controls.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command
question: Why should you collect a tech support file from a suspected PAN-OS victim before upgrading to the fixed version?
options: The upgrade will not install without one
After the reboot into the new version, some logs from the prior installation become inaccessible on the device
It speeds up the upgrade
It deletes the attacker's files
explain: Evidence first, then the fix. Upgrading changes the system you need to examine; the advisory's FAQ says exactly this, and BOD 26-04's forensic triage steps (lesson 11) put collection before patching for the same reason.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
question: Why enforce an outbound allowlist on the firewall in front of a VPN appliance, rather than relying on the appliance's own settings?
options: Appliance settings cannot be changed
It makes the VPN faster
If the appliance is taken over, its own settings are under the attacker's control; a separate device keeps blocking and logging
Allowlists are required by TLS
explain: A control on the compromised box can be switched off by the intruder. A separate enforcement and logging point keeps working, and its blocked-connection logs become detection signals. This is AA24-060B's advice.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
question: Compute: a test set has two problems. Response 1 is 400 tokens, first correct at 100. Response 2 is 800 tokens, first correct at 800. What is the outcome efficiency?
explain: $(100/400 + 800/800)/2 = (0.25 + 1.0)/2 = 0.625$. Response 2 needed all its tokens, so it counts as fully efficient even though it is long.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
question: A sensor driver wants to stop `invoice.exe` from ever running. Where can it do that?
options: In a post-operation file minifilter callback after the EXE is closed
In its process-creation callback, by setting CreationStatus to an error code
In the WFP network filter when the process first connects
In the console, once the alert arrives
explain: The process-creation callback runs before the new process starts, and the documented CreationStatus field lets the driver fail the creation. A network filter or console action can only act after the process is already running.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
question: A sysmon-modular coverage layer shows ATT&CK technique T1055 as 'covered'. What can you conclude?
options: Every process injection on these hosts will be detected
Defender for Endpoint is no longer needed
T1055 events are now blocked
The config collects telemetry that may be useful for T1055; whether it records a given implementation, and whether any detection rule uses it, still needs testing
explain: The project's README states that ATT&CK mappings identify potentially useful telemetry and do not guarantee that every implementation is recorded or that a detection exists. Coverage of data is not coverage of detection.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
question: Your App Control policy runs in enforce mode and you see a 3076 event on one laptop. What does that tell you?
options: The file was blocked
The policy failed to load
The file was allowed by the ISG
That laptop is still running an audit-mode policy (or an additional audit policy), because 3076 is the audit-mode would-be block
explain: 3076 is written only for audit-mode policies; enforced blocks are 3077. A 3076 on a machine you believe is enforced means a policy there is in audit mode, which is worth checking with CiTool -lp and event 3099.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
question: Which control stops AuKill's outdated Process Explorer driver from loading if the file is already on disk?
options: The ASR rule 'Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers'
Sysmon event 6
LAPS
The vulnerable driver blocklist or an App Control driver block policy
explain: Microsoft's ASR reference says that rule prevents writing vulnerable signed drivers but does not stop an existing driver from loading; the blocklist or App Control policy prevents the load. Sysmon only records; LAPS manages passwords.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
question: Which grant should an investigator treat as the most dangerous in a review of consent grants?
options: User.Read delegated, consented by one user
Mail.ReadWrite as an application permission on a non-Microsoft app nobody recognises
openid and profile for a verified Microsoft app
Files.Read delegated, consented by one user
explain: Application permissions work without any user and cover the whole tenant, and write access lets the app change or send mail. Microsoft's playbook places app-only versions of the Mail permissions, and all write-capable app-only permissions, at the top of the review list.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
question: Storm-2372 obtained a PRT through a device it registered. Which response removes that foothold most directly?
options: Resetting the user's password only
Disabling or deleting the attacker-registered device in Entra ID and revoking the user's sessions
Enabling security defaults
Blocking the user's home IP address
explain: Microsoft lists disabling or deleting the device as invalidating its PRT. A password reset invalidates PRTs obtained with the password, but the device remains registered; revoking sessions clears the refresh tokens as well.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
question: After containing an Octo Tempest-style intrusion, which audit activity indicates persistence that survives resetting every compromised user?
options: User registered security info
Set domain authentication (a domain switched to federated)
Reset password (self-service)
Update user
explain: Federating a domain to an attacker's identity provider lets them sign tokens for any user in that domain, independent of user passwords. It must be found and reverted, and the federation settings of every domain reviewed.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: select and poll: readiness that costs O(n) per call
question: A proxy holds 50,000 mostly idle connections and wakes about 1,000 times per second. Which change cuts per-wakeup kernel work the most?
options: Switch from poll to select
Raise FD_SETSIZE to 65536 and keep select
Move to epoll so the kernel keeps the interest set and returns only ready descriptors
Call poll with a timeout of 0
explain: With poll every wakeup copies and scans 50,000 entries, so the scan repeats 1,000 times a second. epoll stores the interest set in the kernel once and each wait touches only ready items. select is worse (bitmap rebuilds, 1024 limit), and a zero timeout only turns waiting into spinning.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
question: A teammate tried 40 reranker configurations on a 50-query public set and reports the best one improved nDCG@10 by +0.035 over the baseline. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it, since +0.035 is larger than typical noise on 50 queries
Re-run the same 40 configurations on the same 50 queries with a different random seed to confirm
Score only the chosen configuration (and the baseline) once on a fresh query set that played no part in the choice
Report the average of all 40 configurations instead of the best one
explain: The +0.035 is a maximum over 40 noisy comparisons, so it is biased upward. In our toy, the best of 20 identical systems already gains about +0.038 on 50 queries from luck alone. Re-running on the same queries cannot remove that selection bias, and averaging all 40 answers a different question. A single evaluation on untouched queries gives an unbiased estimate.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
question: Which practice gives the strongest protection against both adaptive overfitting and contamination for a production search eval?
options: Averaging results over more public benchmarks
A private query set sampled from recent traffic, labeled in-house, read for a few pre-declared decisions and replaced on a schedule
Reporting results with five decimal places
Running the paired t-test with alpha = 0.01 instead of 0.05
explain: Recent private queries cannot be in a model's training data and have not been tuned against. Rotation keeps them from wearing out under repeated reads. More public benchmarks help external validity but stay exposed to contamination; stricter alpha alone does not address reuse.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
question: A non-PIE Linux executable runs with randomize_va_space set to 2. Which part of its memory is still at the same address on every run?
options: The main program's own code
The stack
The heap
Shared libraries such as libc
explain: Stack, heap and libraries are randomized. A non-PIE executable is linked for a fixed address, so its code stays put and remains a dependable source of reusable code. Building with -fPIE -pie lets the kernel move it too.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Memory tagging and hardened allocators against heap bugs
question: With random 4-bit MTE tags, a use-after-free happens to access memory that was re-tagged with the same value the stale pointer carries. What is the chance of this for one access, and what follows?
options: Zero: tags are never reused
1 in 16; the access is not detected, so MTE is probabilistic rather than a guarantee
1 in 256; the CPU detects it later
1 in 2; MTE only checks writes
explain: Four bits give 16 values. A random match goes undetected, which is why MTE is described as a strong probabilistic mitigation, and why allocators choose tags to differ from neighbours where they can.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
question: Which pair of mitigations, combined, covers both the return-address hijack and the function-pointer hijack of earlier lessons?
options: Stack canary and ASLR
A shadow stack (or PAC return signing) plus forward-edge CFI such as CFG or Clang CFI
NX and FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO and a sandbox
explain: Shadow stacks and PAC guard backward edges (returns); CFI, CFG, IBT and BTI guard forward edges (indirect calls and jumps). Canaries and ASLR only hinder, and NX and FORTIFY address different steps.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
question: Eight threads update a shared histogram with 1,000,000 buckets of 8 bytes; updates land on random buckets. What is the best fix?
options: Give each thread a private histogram and merge them at the end
Pad every bucket to 64 bytes
Align the histogram array to 64 bytes
Use a bigger cache line size constant
explain: Padding every bucket would turn 8 MB into 64 MB and wreck cache use for little gain, since random buckets rarely collide. Per-thread histograms (fix 1) remove shared writes entirely, at the cost of 8 copies and one merge. Aligning the array only moves where the boundaries fall.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working
question: You halve B and keep E fixed. Which quantity changes the most?
options: Bytes uploaded per client per round, which doubles
SGD updates per client per round, which doubles
Rounds to the accuracy target, which always halves
The number of clients the server must wait for
explain: Updates per round are E times n_k over B, so halving B doubles them. Communication per round is set by the model size, not by B or E: one download and one upload of the parameters. Whether the extra local work converts into fewer rounds depends on how heterogeneous the clients are, so option C is exactly the trap.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
question: A workload filters images by label 'cat' while queries are photos of dogs, so passing points sit far from each query. Which baseline suffers most?
options: Pre-filtering, because selectivity drops
Post-filtering, because the unfiltered search heads toward the wrong region
Neither, since both are exact
The oracle partition index
explain: This is negative query correlation. Post-filtering's unfiltered search converges near dog photos that fail the filter, and it must expand very far to collect K cats. Pre-filtering's cost depends only on how many records pass, not on where they sit.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: Why is the combinatorial count, not the expert count, the quantity the paper highlights?
options: Because more combinations means more FLOPs
Because routers need at least a billion options to converge
Because GPUs schedule experts by combination
Because each token's computation is a sum over its chosen experts, so more possible subsets means a more precisely targeted mix of knowledge at the same cost
explain: A token's MoE output is the gated sum of its chosen experts. With 120 possible pairs, many different kinds of tokens must share the same pair. With billions of possible 8-subsets of small experts, the token can assemble a closer fit. FLOPs are identical in both designs.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
question: On H100 at $d = 128$, exponentials take about 50% of the matmul time. If FP8 matmuls run at 2x the FP16 rate and MUFU is unchanged, what does that ratio become?
options: 25%, because FP8 values are half the size
50%, unchanged
About 100%
About 200%
explain: $T_{exp}/T_{MMA} = r_{MMA}/(4 d\, r_{exp})$. Doubling $r_{MMA}$ doubles the ratio from 0.5 to 1.0: the exponentials now take as long as the matmuls. The FlashAttention-3 paper says exactly this: "the matmul throughput doubles but the exponential throughput stays the same."

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
question: What is the main reason FlashAttention-4 uses the 2-CTA MMA mode in the backward pass?
options: To double the tensor core FLOPs available to each CTA
To cut shared memory traffic (each CTA stages half of operand B) and halve dQ atomic adds
To make the backward pass deterministic
To fit five accumulators in tensor memory
explain: The backward pass is limited by shared memory bandwidth (3328 vs 2560 cycles). Pairing CTAs means each stages half of B, and the dS exchange lets each CTA own half of the dQ tile, halving atomics. Peak FLOPs are unchanged, and determinism comes from the separate semaphore mode.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
question: Doubling Euler steps from 8 to 16 on the toy cut the endpoint error from about 0.135 to about 0.067. What does that ratio indicate?
options: Error is roughly proportional to step size, so Euler is first order
Euler is a second-order method
The flow is straight
The network is overfitting
explain: Halving h roughly halved the error, which is first-order behavior: global error proportional to h. A second-order method like Heun would cut it by about 4x.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
question: You fix the race by making the increment one atomic step (and remove tmp from the spec): `Inc(p) == pc[p] = "inc" /\ x' = x + 1 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "done"]`. What does TLC report for N = 2?
options: Still a violation, because two processes can run Inc in the same step
No error: every step increments x by 1, so x = 2 once both are done
A deadlock error, because Inc can never be enabled
It cannot check it, since x' = x + 1 is an assignment
explain: Next allows exactly one process to take one step at a time, so nothing interleaves inside Inc. TLC confirms it: 4 distinct states, no error (8 states for N = 3). In PlusCal the fix is to put the read and write under one label.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
question: In TwoPhase, the TM receives a Prepared message, which changes only tmPrepared. What does TCommit see under the refinement mapping?
options: A Prepare step by that RM
A stuttering step, because rmState is unchanged
A violation, since TCommit has no TM
Nothing: refinement checking skips steps that change hidden variables
explain: The mapping exposes only rmState. A step that leaves rmState unchanged maps to a stuttering step, which every TLA+ spec allows. TLC does not skip it; it checks that it is a stutter.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: A small Rust function parses a length-prefixed packet using unsafe pointer arithmetic, with inputs up to 64 bytes. You want a counterexample if any input can cause out-of-bounds access, with minimal annotation. Which fits best?
options: TLA+ with TLC
P
TLAPS
Kani with a harness over any 64-byte input
explain: This is a code-level, bounded question about one function: exactly what Kani's harnesses and kani::any() are for, and Kani checks for undefined behavior in unsafe code. TLA+, P and TLAPS work on design models, not on the Rust code.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: A team turns on FP8 GEMMs for every linear layer and expects peak memory to halve. It barely changes. Why?
options: FP8 tensors are padded to 16 bits in memory
Most memory is master weights, gradients, optimizer moments and activations that FP8 GEMM inputs do not touch
The amax history uses more memory than the weights
Tensor cores cannot read FP8 from memory
explain: FP8 GEMMs change compute, not the 12 to 16 bytes per parameter of training state. FP8-LM cut memory by moving the gradient and first moment to FP8 and the master weight and second moment to FP16, and DeepSeek-V3 caches activations in FP8.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: Why does the recipe use 16x16 2D blocks for weights but 1x16 blocks for activations and gradients?
options: 2D blocks are faster for every tensor
Activations cannot be transposed
1x16 blocks are required by E4M3
Weights are reused in both Fprop and Dgrad (transposed), so a scale shared over a square block keeps the two quantized copies identical; activations and gradients benefit more from finer 1x16 scaling
explain: The chain-rule mismatch matters most for weights, and weights can adapt to coarser scaling during training. The report found training less sensitive to inconsistency in activations, so they keep the more accurate 1x16 blocks.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
question: A server has a single active client and commit_delay = 2000 microseconds with commit_siblings = 0. What happens to that client?
options: Each commit gets about 2 ms slower and throughput drops, since nobody else can join
Nothing, since commit_delay is ignored with one client
Commits get faster because flushes are batched
Commits become asynchronous
explain: With commit_siblings = 0 the sibling check always passes, so the lone leader sleeps 2 ms before every flush with no one to share it. That is pure added latency. The default commit_siblings = 5 exists to skip the sleep when joiners are unlikely.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Coverage-guided fuzzing: how AFL's edge bitmap steers mutation
question: What does the shift in prev_location = cur_location >> 1 achieve?
options: It makes A then B land in a different slot from B then A, and keeps a block jumping to itself distinct
It halves the map size
It randomises block numbers at run time
It counts how many times each block ran
explain: Without the shift, A XOR B equals B XOR A, and A XOR A is zero for every block, so direction and tight loops would be lost. Shifting the previous location breaks that symmetry.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
question: What does libFuzzer's -merge=1 MIN corpus/ do?
options: Copies into MIN only the inputs from corpus/ that add coverage not already in MIN
Deletes crashing inputs from corpus/
Merges two fuzzers into one process
Minimises each input to its smallest size
explain: The docs: inputs from the second and later directories that trigger new coverage are merged into the first. It shrinks a corpus to a coverage-equivalent subset; per-input shrinking is a different feature (-minimize_crash or reduce_inputs).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing beyond C: Go, Rust, Python and property-based testing
question: What is the oracle in the Hypothesis example?
options: The property decode(encode(name)) == name, which must hold for every generated string
A crash or hang
AddressSanitizer
Code coverage
explain: Property-based testing finds wrong answers, not just crashes. The round-trip property caught a failure that raises nothing at all: the two-character string U+0080 then "0" decodes back as U+0080 alone, a silently wrong answer. The cause is that the length byte counts characters instead of bytes.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
question: Why did OSS-Fuzz's long-running SQLite fuzzing miss the bug Big Sleep found?
options: The OSS-Fuzz harness was not built with the generate_series extension, and AFL on the right binary did not find it in 150 CPU-hours
SQLite has no fuzz targets
The bug only occurs on Windows
Fuzzers cannot find stack bugs
explain: The Big Sleep post: the harness configuration left the extension out, and a dedicated AFL attempt with the needed keywords still failed. Reach and difficulty, not lack of fuzzing, explain the miss.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
question: You are building a structure whose correctness depends on the triangle inequality (lesson 5). Which distance is unsafe to plug in?
options: Levenshtein
Indel
Optimal string alignment (OSA)
True Damerau-Levenshtein
explain: OSA violates the triangle inequality: CA to AC is 1, AC to ABC is 1, but CA to ABC is 3. A search structure that prunes with that inequality could skip a real match. Levenshtein, Indel and true Damerau-Levenshtein are metrics.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
question: A plate solver's answer is described by pointing, rotation and field of view. How many continuous numbers is that?
explain: Pointing on the sky is 2 numbers (RA and Dec), plus 1 rotation angle, plus 1 scale. Lang et al. describe the hypothesis space as continuous and four-dimensional, which is why exhaustive search is impractical.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
question: During verification, star 3 of a true alignment is a satellite with no catalog counterpart. Why does the foreground model include a distractor term d instead of putting all probability on the predicted catalog stars?
options: Without it, any single unmatched star would give a ratio near zero and could veto a correct alignment
To make the computation faster
Because the background model also has a distractor term
To make the false positive rate exactly zero
explain: If F gave zero probability to stars away from predictions, one artifact, planet or catalog gap would multiply K by almost zero. The mixture with d = 0.25 caps the penalty at about -0.6 in log10 per stray star, so real images with junk still solve.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
question: Near the Louvre, 7-character geohash cells are about 153 m tall and 100.5 m wide. Which precision should a 100 m radius query use with a 3 x 3 covering?
options: Length 6, because longer geohashes are always slower
Length 7, the longest whose cells are at least 100 m on both sides here
Length 8, because smaller cells mean fewer false positives
Any length works, since 9 cells always cover the circle
explain: Length 7 cells are just over 100 m in both directions, so the 3 x 3 block is guaranteed to cover the circle with the least overfetch. Length 8 cells (about 19 to 38 m) are smaller than the radius, so 9 of them miss matches. Length 6 is correct but reads many more candidates.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
question: You resize a 4-pixel row to 2 pixels with nearest neighbour. Which source indices does the half-pixel convention read, and which does the floor convention read?
options: Both read 0 and 2, because floor of a half-integer rounds down
Half-pixel reads 1 and 3; floor reads 0 and 2
Half-pixel reads 0 and 2; floor reads 1 and 3
Both read 1 and 3, because the half is added before scaling
explain: Half-pixel: floor((0 + 0.5) x 2) = 1 and floor((1 + 0.5) x 2) = 3. Floor convention: 0 x 2 = 0 and 1 x 2 = 2. At this scale the two conventions never agree on a single pixel, and the half-pixel one reads the source pixel that covers the output pixel's center.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
question: A pipeline resizes 64 crops of 256x256 one at a time, synchronizing after each to check for errors. Measurements show the GPU busy about 6 percent of the time. What is the single best change?
options: Switch the interpolation from bilinear to nearest to halve the arithmetic
Increase the block size so each kernel has more parallelism
Use pinned host memory for the output buffers
Batch all 64 crops into one launch and synchronize once at the end
explain: At 0.44 microseconds of kernel work against 6.7 microseconds of exposed launch overhead, utilization near 6 percent is exactly what the model predicts. Removing 63 launches and 63 synchronizations is the only change that attacks the dominant term. Interpolation arithmetic and block size are irrelevant when the kernel is not the bottleneck, and pinned memory addresses host transfers, not launch overhead.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
question: Which workload benefits most from expandable_segments?
options: Batched inference where the batch size changes slightly between iterations
A model whose tensor shapes are identical every iteration
A job that only allocates 1 KiB tensors
A program that shares every CUDA tensor with worker processes via IPC
explain: Fixed segments work well when sizes repeat exactly. Drifting batch sizes create slightly larger tensors that leave slivers in old segments. Small-only workloads already pack into 2 MiB segments, and IPC sharing is not supported for expandable memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
question: A kernel reads `x[i * 4]` (floats) for consecutive `i` across a warp, and each element is used once. What fraction of fetched bytes is useful, ignoring cache reuse?
explain: Threads are 16 bytes apart, so each 32-byte sector holds 2 requested floats: 16 sectors per warp for 128 useful bytes. 128 / (16 x 32) = 25%.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
question: Why does Nsight Compute define Memory Throughput as the maximum over its constituent counters instead of their sum?
options: Because summing could exceed 100 percent and look wrong
Because L1, L2 and DRAM counters are collected in different replay passes and cannot be added
Because a throughput is meant to say how close some unit got to its own peak, and the binding constraint is the unit nearest its own ceiling
Because DRAM always dominates the other memory units
explain: The metrics guide defines a throughput as how close a portion of the GPU came to peak rate, and says throughput metrics return the maximum percentage of their constituents, chosen to represent the parts of the pipeline that govern peak performance. The slowest relative unit is what limits you, so the max is the meaningful aggregate; the breakdown then names which unit it was.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
question: A, B and C are allocated with cudaMallocManaged (unified memory, readable by host and device). The host launches `vecAdd<<<4, 256>>>(A, B, C)` and on the very next line prints `C[0]`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: a kernel launch blocks until the kernel finishes
The launch is asynchronous, so the host may read C before the kernel has written it; call cudaDeviceSynchronize() first
Only block 0 has finished by then, but C[0] belongs to block 0 so it is fine
Unified memory cannot be read by the host after a launch
explain: The guide states that kernel launches are asynchronous with respect to the host thread: the kernel may not have finished, or even started. Its unified memory example calls cudaDeviceSynchronize() before the host touches the results. Blocks also have no guaranteed order, so 'block 0 finishes first' is not a safe assumption either.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
question: You port a CUDA kernel to Metal and dispatch it with `dispatchThreads` for exactly N threads. The CUDA version had `if (i >= N) return;` at the top. What should you do with that check?
options: Keep it: Metal always rounds the grid up to whole threadgroups
It becomes redundant: with nonuniform threadgroups Metal launches exactly N threads, though keeping it is harmless
Replace it with threadgroup_barrier, which skips out-of-range threads
Change it to `if (i >= N * threadExecutionWidth)`
explain: dispatchThreads takes the total thread count and creates smaller edge threadgroups, so no thread position exceeds the data. Apple notes you do not need the position check in that case. With dispatchThreadgroups you would need it, just as in CUDA.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
question: In the map step, one batch returns only points with importance score 0. What happens to them?
options: They are filtered out before the reduce step
They are kept but sorted last
They trigger a retry with a larger batch
They are replaced by raw text chunks
explain: Both the paper and the repo drop score-0 answers. If every map answer scores 0, the repo returns a canned "I do not know" unless general knowledge is explicitly allowed.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
question: A team's math verifier compares strings after stripping whitespace. Training stalls on problems whose labels are fractions like 1/2. What is the most likely bug?
options: The KL coefficient is too small
The group size is too large
The policy writes equivalent forms such as 0.5 that the verifier scores 0, so correct reasoning is never rewarded
The verifier gives reward to wrong answers
explain: String matching treats 0.5 and 1/2 as different. Correct solutions get reward 0, so the policy receives no signal on exactly those problems. Normalizing answers (or checking mathematical equivalence) fixes it.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
question: R1-Zero's response length grew to thousands of tokens without any length reward. Which explanation fits the mechanism of GRPO with an outcome reward?
options: The KL penalty rewards longer outputs
The format reward pays per token
Outputs that reasoned longer were more often correct, so they got positive advantages and the habits that produced them were reinforced
The verifier counts reasoning steps
explain: The reward checks only the answer and the tags. Whatever behavior raises the chance of a correct answer relative to sibling samples (here, longer reflective reasoning) gets reinforced through the group-relative advantage.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: Updates for a 6-stop trip: seq 2 delay 60, seq 4 SKIPPED, nothing else. Scheduled times at seq 5 and 6 are 09:10:00 and 09:20:00. What are the predictions at seq 5 and 6?
options: No prediction, because SKIPPED ends propagation
09:10:00 and 09:20:00, because the skip resets delay to 0
09:11:00 at seq 5 only, delay never travels more than two stops
explain: SKIPPED does not stop delay propagation, so the 60 s from seq 2 carries past the skipped stop to seq 5 and 6. Only another SCHEDULED update or NO_DATA changes the carried value.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Inside the PMU: event selectors, counters and overflow
question: You run `perf stat -e r1a8:u` instead of `r1a8`. What changes in the event-select register?
options: The OS bit is cleared, so occurrences in kernel mode are not counted
The event code becomes 0x1A9
The INT bit is set, so it starts sampling
Nothing; modifiers only change how perf prints the result
explain: Modifiers like :u and :k map to privilege filtering (exclude_kernel, exclude_user). On x86 that becomes the OS and USR bits of the event-select register. The event code and umask stay 0xA8 and 0x01.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
question: Which observer needs no physical access and no code on the target machine?
options: A power probe on a smart card
A JavaScript program in another browser tab
A client timing a TLS server's replies over the network
A process on a sibling hyperthread
explain: Only remote timing works purely over the network. JavaScript and sibling processes are co-located code; power probes need physical access.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: CPU caches as a shared resource: Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe
question: Why does constant-time code defeat both Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe?
options: Its memory addresses and branches do not depend on secrets, so the cache footprint is the same for every secret
It disables the cache while it runs
It runs faster than the spy can measure
It flushes the cache after every operation
explain: Cache attacks observe which lines were used. If that set of lines does not depend on the secret, the observation carries no information about it.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: The family grows: Foreshadow, MDS, Downfall, Zenbleed, Inception
question: Zenbleed leaked data without any cache timing measurement. What made that possible?
options: It used Rowhammer to flip register bits
The faulty rollback left the attacker's vector register referring to register-file contents written by other code, so the data could simply be read
It disabled the cache
It needed physical access to the CPU
explain: Ormandy describes it as a use-after-free in the register file: the stale data became architecturally visible in the attacker's own register. No covert channel was needed, which is why it was fast.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
question: Why can checkm8 never be fixed on affected devices, unlike a bug in iOS?
options: Apple chose not to patch it
It needs a network connection that cannot be blocked
The exploit is persistent across reboots
It lives in SecureROM, read-only boot code inside the chip, which firmware updates cannot change
explain: CERT/CC: SecureROM is read-only, so it cannot be patched. The mitigating factors are physical access, DFU mode, and that the exploit does not persist across reboots.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: A latency-critical service shows p99 spikes on allocation-heavy requests and a fast-rising compact_stall. THP is enabled=always, defrag=always. Which change targets the spikes while keeping most THP benefit?
options: Set defrag to defer so faults fall back to small pages and khugepaged collapses later
Set max_ptes_none to 0
Raise khugepaged pages_to_scan
Switch enabled to madvise and defrag to always
explain: The spikes come from direct compaction inside page faults. defer stops faults from stalling and leaves the work to kcompactd and khugepaged. max_ptes_none and pages_to_scan only affect khugepaged, not fault stalls, and madvise mode with defrag=always still stalls in any region the app marks.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
question: A hybrid's Mamba layer state is 1 MiB and one token of one attention layer's KV is 2 KiB. Under vLLM's rule that one attention block must hold at least one Mamba state's bytes, what is the smallest attention block size?
options: 16 tokens
256 tokens
512 tokens
1,024 tokens
explain: 1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes; divided by 2,048 bytes per token that is 512 tokens. Blocks that large make prefix-cache hits coarse, which is why vLLM's design doc calls 400-plus-token blocks too large.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
question: With k = 60, BM25 returns documents scoring 41.2 and 40.9 at ranks 1 and 2, and a second run with a different tokenizer returns 9.3 and 2.1 at ranks 1 and 2. How do the RRF contributions of these four positions compare?
options: The first run contributes far more because its scores are larger
Rank 1 gets 1/61 and rank 2 gets 1/62 in both runs; raw score gaps are ignored
The second run contributes more because its gap between ranks is bigger
They cannot be compared without normalizing first
explain: RRF uses only positions. That makes it immune to score scales (good) but blind to the fact that the second run is much more confident about its top hit (information lost). Bruch et al. argue this loss of score information is one reason a tuned convex combination can beat RRF.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
question: Your corpus index was built with Contriever. A colleague proposes embedding the hypothetical documents with a different, stronger embedding model to save effort. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, any embedding model works with any index
Only latency increases
The LLM must then be retrained
The vector lands in a different embedding space, so inner products with the indexed Contriever vectors are meaningless
explain: HyDE relies on document-document similarity inside one space. The hypothetical passage must be encoded by the same encoder f that encoded the corpus, otherwise the averaged vector and the index vectors are not comparable.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
question: In the tank loop, which component turns a decision into a physical change?
options: The sensor
The HMI
The actuator (the pump)
The setpoint
explain: The actuator acts on the process. Sensors measure, the controller decides, the HMI lets humans supervise, and setpoints are the desired values the controller compares against.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
question: Decode this request: `00 05 00 00 00 06 01 05 00 00 FF 00`. What does it ask for? (Function 05 uses 0xFF00 for ON and 0x0000 for OFF.)
options: Read coil 0
Write single coil 0 to ON
Write single register 0 to 65280
An exception reply
explain: Function code 0x05 is Write Single Coil; address 0x0000; value 0xFF00 means ON. In the tank this could be the pump's run coil, which is why a monitor should flag any write from a host that is not the HMI.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
question: In the 2015 attack, which control would most directly have blocked the breaker operations?
options: Antivirus signatures for BlackEnergy on substation RTUs
Requiring multi-factor authentication and operator-controlled, time-limited approval for any remote access into the control network
Encrypting the historian
Faster patching of office PCs
explain: The breakers were opened by humans using stolen credentials over VPN and legitimate tools. Strong MFA plus approval-gated, time-limited remote access attacks that path directly; the investigators could not tie the outage to BlackEnergy's capabilities.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Watching OT: asset inventory and passive monitoring
question: A consultant proposes an aggressive network scan of all PLCs to build the inventory during production. What does NIST advise?
options: Go ahead: scans are harmless
Prefer passive discovery from SPAN ports or taps; schedule any active scanning during planned outages because probes may destabilise devices
Scan only at night while running
Unplug each PLC and inspect it
explain: NIST: passive scans add no traffic; active scans 'may cause device instability or interfere with the device process state' and should be scheduled in planned outages.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML Signature from zero: canonical form, digests and SignedInfo
question: In an enveloped XML signature, what does SignatureValue directly sign?
options: The whole SAML response
Only the NameID
The certificate in KeyInfo
The canonical SignedInfo element, which contains the digest of the referenced element
explain: SignatureValue covers SignedInfo. The referenced element is protected indirectly, through the DigestValue inside SignedInfo. KeyInfo is not covered unless a Reference points at it, which is one reason a verifier must not trust a key just because the message carries it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML signature wrapping: the verifier and the app read different parts
question: Which fix closes the class of bug rather than one variant?
options: Reject responses whose first Assertion has no Signature child
Blocklist the Extensions element
Use a longer RSA key
Have the verifier return the exact element it verified, and make the app use only that element
explain: Blocking one wrapper position or element name leaves others: the paper found a new variant against Salesforce despite specific countermeasures. Binding the decision to the verified element (only process what is hashed) removes the gap itself. Key length is irrelevant: the crypto was never broken.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
question: Why does an OIDC Logout Token forbid the nonce claim?
options: Nonces are too long
Because logout tokens are not signed
Because the IdP does not know the nonce
So a logout token can never be accepted in place of an ID token
explain: The specification prohibits nonce in logout tokens; ID tokens from an authentication request carry one. Together with the events claim, that keeps the two JWT types from being confused.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Detecting forged federation tokens and recovering trust
question: Why does Microsoft's guidance rotate the AD FS token-signing certificate twice after a compromise?
options: Because the first rotation always fails
To confuse the attacker
Because SAML requires two certificates
Because after one rotation the old certificate is kept as a secondary and still works; a second rotation pushes it out
explain: Normal rollover keeps the previous certificate for a grace period so relying parties can catch up. During a compromise that grace period is exactly what the attacker needs, so the old certificate must be forced out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Joiner, mover, leaver: the lifecycle and how access creeps
question: A contractor was onboarded directly in three applications and never appears in the HR system. What is the most important control to add?
options: Give the contractor a longer password
Wait for the HR leaver event to remove their access
Assign a named employee sponsor and an expiry date, and include the accounts in reviews
Convert the contractor's accounts to shared accounts
explain: No HR record means no leaver event will ever fire. A sponsor makes a person accountable, and an expiry date makes removal the default. Shared accounts make accountability worse, not better.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
